title: Observing the Planets

learn.summary: Five planets are naked-eye objects known since antiquity: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn. Planets shine with steadier light than twinkling stars and always sit near the ecliptic — two clues that let you pick them out instantly. Their positions change week to week, which is exactly what 'planet' (Greek for wanderer) means.

do: Identify every planet currently visible in your evening sky this week using a planetarium app to verify your naked-eye guesses.

children.title: Venus & Its Phases

learn.summary: Venus is the third-brightest object in the sky (after Sun and Moon), reaching magnitude -4.6 — bright enough to cast faint shadows and be seen in daylight. Because it orbits inside Earth's orbit, it shows Moon-like phases, which Galileo saw in 1610 as decisive evidence against the pure Earth-centered model. Even steady binoculars can show its crescent.

do: Next time Venus is visible, find it in twilight before full darkness — note that it appears before any star does.

children.title: Jupiter's Moons

learn.summary: Any binoculars reveal up to four star-like points flanking Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, the moons Galileo discovered in January 1610. They visibly rearrange within hours as they orbit (Io circles in just 1.8 days) — the first direct proof that not everything orbits Earth. Jupiter itself outshines every star.

do: When Jupiter is next visible, brace binoculars against a wall or fence and count its moons; sketch their positions, then check again the following night to see the change.

children.title: Saturn's Rings

learn.summary: Saturn's rings — mostly water ice, spanning 280,000 km but often less than a kilometer thick — need about 25x magnification to resolve clearly, making them the most famous 'first telescope view' in astronomy. The ring tilt cycles over Saturn's 29-year orbit, from wide open to edge-on invisible. Naked-eye, Saturn is a steady golden 'star' of about magnitude +0.5.

do: Locate Saturn naked-eye during its next apparition and note its steady, yellowish light; if you can access any telescope (a club star party counts), make seeing the rings your goal this season.

children.title: Conjunctions & Alignments

learn.summary: Because all planets travel the ecliptic, they periodically pair up in conjunctions — sometimes spectacularly, as in December 2020 when Jupiter and Saturn passed within 0.1 degrees, their closest since 1623. The Moon makes a conjunction with some planet almost every week, offering easy photo opportunities. These events are predictable decades ahead, so plan for them.

do: Find the next Moon-planet conjunction within the coming month using an app or almanac, and observe or photograph the pairing.

children.title: Retrograde Motion

learn.summary: Outer planets normally drift eastward against the stars, but around opposition they appear to reverse for weeks — an illusion caused by faster-moving Earth overtaking them on the inside track. Explaining retrograde loops tortured astronomers for 1,500 years of epicycles until Copernicus dissolved the problem. You can verify it yourself with a few weeks of patience.

do: Pick Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn and record its position against background stars once a week for a month — plot the points and see the drift with your own data.
